label: Extreme Points And Faces
notes: Open by positioning faces as the internal counterpart to support halfspaces. The lecture will keep two questions in sync: which pieces of the boundary can be certified by segments, and which pieces can be exposed by a linear functional?

label: Segment Test
notes: Use the chord picture slowly. A point is extreme only when every attempt to write it as a strict convex average collapses to the same point. The edge point fails because the segment endpoints are different feasible points.

label: Face Definition
notes: The definition is stronger than convex subset. A face inherits every endpoint of a segment whose relative interior it captures. This endpoint-forcing property is why faces behave like honest boundary pieces instead of arbitrary convex slices.

label: Exposed Face
notes: Connect this slide back to support functions. A vector c scores every point of C, and the maximizers form an exposed face. Generic directions usually expose points; special normals can expose higher-dimensional faces. Ask learners to identify the exposed set before naming it, then point out that the certificate is the normal vector plus the attained support value.

label: Polygon And Polytope Examples
notes: For polytopes, faces become active-constraint patterns. One active supporting inequality may select an edge, two independent active inequalities may select a vertex, and the zero support vector leaves the whole set active. Use the examples to make the rank of active normals visible: geometry, algebra, and the solver's active-set report are the same object.

label: Nonexposed Warning
notes: Pause on the warning because it prevents a common overreach. Exposure is a powerful certificate, but not every face or extreme point has such a certificate in the original set. Later density results recover exposed approximations, not literal equality.

label: Minimal Face
notes: Introduce the minimal face as the unique cell that contains a point in its relative interior. In computation this often means reading the active constraints and then checking a relative-interior witness rather than guessing from a drawing.

label: Faces Under Intersections
notes: Use this as the algebra of facial structure. Intersections move downward in the lattice, faces of faces remain faces of the original set, and the smallest face above a collection is obtained as a lattice join.

label: Recession And Lineality
notes: Separate finite boundary pieces from behavior at infinity. Half-line faces give extreme directions, while lineality means every candidate can move both forward and backward, destroying isolated extreme structure unless we quotient it away. Emphasize that recession data is not a side case for unbounded sets; it is the part of the facial story that records how the set escapes to infinity.

label: Decomposition Into Extremes And Rays
notes: State the finite-dimensional Krein-Milman intuition in practical language. Closed convex sets with no lines are built from extreme points and extreme directions; bounded sets need only extreme points, while exposed data may require closure. Keep the message computational: if a representation has too many generators, the theorem tells us which generators are structurally meaningful and which ones can be compressed away.

label: Numerical Face Certificate
notes: This slide turns definitions into a solver-side checklist. For a polyhedron, the active equalities define a candidate face, inactive slacks certify relative interior, and support residuals explain which linear functional exposes the face. Walk through the JSON-style certificate: active rows, rank, slack signs, and objective ties are all inspectable, so the face claim can be audited numerically.

label: Rule Ledger
notes: The ledger is the memory aid for the section. Keep face, exposed face, extreme point, extreme direction, recession cone, and lineality in separate rows so the diagnostics do not blur together. Encourage students to read across each row as a contract: what certificate proves the object exists, what computation finds it, and what failure mode would invalidate it.

label: Recap
notes: Close with the governing habit: classify the boundary piece by the certificate it admits. Segment tests detect extreme points, support tests expose faces, active constraints compute minimal faces, and recession tests identify what happens at infinity.
